name: rq-text
text: How do participants dynamically calibrate reliance on self vs. AI in repeated human-AI decisions, and how does a localized AI error shock reshape that reliance path?

name: H1-body
text: Reliance should follow repeated feedback about relative self-AI performance.

name: H2-body
text: Concentrated AI errors should reduce later AI adoption compared with balanced errors.

name: H3-body

name: H4-body

name: central-text
text: Do equal performance histories produce equal reliance recovery, or do AI errors leave a longer shadow?
textPreview: Do equal performance histories produce equal reliance recovery, or do AI errors leave a longer shadow?

text:
Here I want to make the questions explicit before moving into the treatment map.
The overall question is how participants learn between self and AI in a repeated feedback environment. Every round gives them information about both sides, so the key outcome is not a one-time attitude. It is the reliance path.
H1 asks whether people update reliance based on relative performance. If AI repeatedly performs better than self, AI adoption should rise. If self performs better, AI adoption should fall.
H2 then introduces the shock: if AI errors are concentrated in one stage rather than spread out, do people reduce later AI adoption even when overall performance is matched?
H3 asks what happens after the shock is over. If people recalibrate fully, reliance should recover when AI performance recovers. If there is path dependence or trust lag, reliance may stay low.
H4 asks whether timing matters. Early shocks can shape initial calibration, while mid shocks can break a reliance relationship that has already started to form.
H5 is the source-asymmetry test. It is not only whether AI is punished more immediately. It is whether AI is forgiven more slowly than self after comparable errors.
So the central test is whether equal performance histories lead to equal recovery, or whether AI errors leave a longer shadow.
